intro: Discovery tells you what is worth doing; scoping decides exactly what you will do, by when, with whose help, and how everyone will know it worked. A good scope is the difference between a pilot that ends in a confident yes or no and one that drifts for months. This lesson covers choosing between a proof of concept, a pilot and a production project, writing success criteria that cannot be argued about later, drawing scope boundaries, listing the customer's own commitments, building a timeline with go/no-go gates, keeping a risk register, and handling change without losing control.
objectives: Choose between a proof of concept, a pilot and a production engagement
Write measurable success criteria and explicit in-scope and out-of-scope lists
Record assumptions and customer dependencies with owners and dates
Build a timeboxed plan with milestones and go/no-go gates
Maintain a risk register and a lightweight change-control process

sections.heading: Proof of concept, pilot or production?

rows: Can this work at all technically?
Does it deliver value in their real workflow?
Real data, a limited group of real users
Can it run for everyone, reliably and supported?

blocks.text: Match the engagement to the open question. If feasibility is genuinely uncertain (can we extract fields from these scanned forms at all?), run a short POC first. If feasibility is clear and the doubt is about value and adoption, go straight to a pilot with real users, because a POC on sample data proves nothing about the workflow. Many stalled AI projects are endless POCs: technically impressive, never touching a real user.

Turn the discovery metric into criteria that are specific, measurable, owned and time-bound, and write down what you are explicitly not doing. An out-of-scope list is as important as the in-scope one: it is what you point to when someone asks for one more feature in week four.

blocks.caption: A pilot plan as a reviewable document (fields are illustrative)
blocks.code:
pilot: motor-claims-clause-assistant
duration_weeks: 6
users: 12 claims handlers in the Leeds team
success_criteria:
  primary: median handling time for pilot users down >= 30% vs 2-week baseline
  guardrails:
    - clause-lookup accuracy >= 95% on a 200-case expert-reviewed set
    - no increase in escalation rate
    - weekly active use >= 80% of pilot users by week 5
in_scope:
  - motor policies, English-language PDFs
  - read-only access to the claims view
  - web app behind company SSO
out_of_scope:
  - home and commercial policies
  - writing back to the claims system
  - mobile app
decision: go/no-go for wider rollout at end of week 6, sponsor decides

blocks.text: Agree what happens on a 'no' as well as a 'yes'. If the pilot misses its criteria, a clear stop with lessons learned is a good outcome; a vague extension is not.
Most pilot delays are caused by things the customer must provide, not by engineering. List every dependency with an owner and a date, and treat late dependencies as schedule changes, visibly.

rows: Build slips one week per week late
No production data in app until approved

blocks.text: Also write down **assumptions**: things you believe but have not verified, such as "PDFs contain selectable text, not scanned images" or "the claims view refreshes nightly". Verify the riskiest ones in the first week; a wrong assumption found in week five is a crisis, found in week one it is a plan change.

items: **Week 0: kickoff.** Confirm scope, success criteria, dependencies, communication rhythm and decision makers.
**Week 1: foundations.** Access, data samples, baseline measurement, riskiest assumptions tested.
**Weeks 2-3: first working version** with real data, shown to users; evaluation set built with experts.
**Gate (end of week 3):** is it on track to meet criteria? Adjust, continue or stop.
**Weeks 4-5: users on it daily**, weekly iterations, security approval, monitoring in place.
**Week 6: measure and decide.** Compare against baseline, present evidence, sponsor decides go or no-go.

blocks.text: Estimate in ranges and say what drives the uncertainty ("2-4 weeks, depending on whether the forms are scanned"). When you cannot estimate at all, schedule a short **spike**, a timeboxed investigation whose only output is the information needed to estimate.

Keep a short **risk register** from day one: each risk with likelihood, impact, mitigation and owner, reviewed in the weekly status. Typical FDE risks are data access, data quality, security approval, user adoption, scope creep and key-person availability on the customer side. Writing a risk down and sharing it is itself a mitigation: it turns a future surprise into a known, owned issue.

Change will come: a new stakeholder, a new use case, a discovery that the data is worse than expected. Handle it explicitly. Write the proposed change, its effect on timeline, criteria and effort, and get the sponsor's decision: swap it for something else in scope, extend, or defer it to the next phase. Saying "yes, and here is what moves" is how you stay helpful without losing the pilot.
Silent scope creep is the most common way good pilots fail: each small addition is reasonable, together they make the deadline impossible, and the decision meeting arrives with nothing finished.

Commercial engagements wrap the plan in a **statement of work** (SOW) agreed between the companies. As an FDE you usually help draft its technical parts. Make sure it contains the objective, scope and out-of-scope lists, deliverables, success criteria, customer responsibilities, timeline and milestones, acceptance process, assumptions, and how changes are handled. Anything vague in the SOW becomes a disagreement later; anything technical that is promised must be something you know you can deliver.

practice.title: Scope the pilot from your discovery
steps: Take the discovery summary from the previous lesson's practice and decide whether the next step is a POC or a pilot, with one sentence of justification.
Write the pilot plan in the YAML structure above: users, duration, primary metric, guardrails, in-scope and out-of-scope lists, decision.
List at least five customer dependencies with owners, dates and the impact of each being late.
List three assumptions and how you would test each in week one.
Draw a six-week timeline with a mid-point gate and a final decision meeting.
Write a risk register with five risks and a change request for a plausible new feature, showing what would move.

focus: POC for feasibility, pilot for value with real users, production for everyone.
Success criteria: specific, measured against a baseline, owned, dated.
Out-of-scope list is your protection against creep.
Customer dependencies cause most delays: owner and date for each.
Gates and a final decision meeting; agree what a 'no' looks like.
Every change gets a visible trade-off and a sponsor decision.

items.syntax: dependency | owner | needed by | if late
assumption | how to test | by when

items.desc: Timeboxed investigation to enable an estimate

pitfalls: Endless POCs on sample data that never meet a real user.
Success criteria like 'users like it' that cannot be measured.
No out-of-scope list, so every request seems reasonable.
Treating late customer dependencies as your problem silently.
Extending a failing pilot instead of stopping with lessons learned.

quiz.q: Feasibility is clear, but nobody knows whether claims handlers will adopt the tool. What should you propose?
options: A pilot with real users and real data
A longer proof of concept on sample data
A full production rollout to all teams
A research report on AI adoption
quiz.explain: The open question is value and adoption, which only real users in their workflow can answer; a POC on samples cannot.

quiz.q: Which success criterion is best written?
options: Median handling time down 30% vs baseline by week 6
Users find the assistant helpful and easy
The AI is accurate most of the time
The pilot goes well overall
quiz.explain: It names the metric, the comparison, the size of change and the date, so nobody can argue about it later.

quiz.q: In week four the sponsor asks to add home insurance policies. What is the right response?
options: Show the effect on timeline and criteria and ask what to swap or defer
Agree immediately to keep the sponsor happy
Refuse because it was not in the SOW
Add it quietly and work weekends
quiz.explain: Explicit change control keeps you helpful while protecting the pilot: the sponsor decides with the trade-off visible.

quiz.q: Why test the riskiest assumptions in week one?
options: A wrong assumption found early is a plan change, not a crisis
Assumptions expire after the first week
Security reviews require it
It shortens the statement of work
quiz.explain: Discovering that PDFs are scans or data is missing in week one leaves time to adapt; in week five it sinks the pilot.

quiz.q: Access to the claims database arrives two weeks late. How should it be handled?
options: As a visible schedule change tied to the dependency's owner
By using production credentials from a colleague
By hiding the delay until the final demo
By skipping the evaluation to catch up
quiz.explain: Dependencies have owners and dates; when they slip, the timeline moves and everyone should see why.
